question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
question.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2-6t \\ y=1+3t \\ z=-5+2t\end{aligned}
$$

 
for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2-6t \\ 1+3t \\ -5+2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6t \\ 3t \\ 2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(2,1,-5)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨-6,3,2⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{-6}=\frac{y-1}{3}=\frac{z-(-5)}{2}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{-6}=\frac{y-1}{3}=\frac{z+5}{2}.
$$

Two source defects remain: q-105261 incorrectly labels a row scaling as -1/2 instead of +1/2, although its final answer is correct; q-127043 offers two mathematically valid radio choices, options 1 and 2, which are opposite direction vectors. Its worked solution explicitly supports option 1. Independently: q-105261 has u=-b-2c, so s=-1, t=-2 and st=2. In q-34142 and q-105291, the selected vectors equal -3a1 and a1/3 respectively. In q-34276, a3=a1-a2 proves dependence, so only III is true. In q-105315, the determinant is -6, proving independence and making II and III true. In q-36023 and q-127002, constant coordinates give the base point and coefficients of t give the direction vector. Those coefficients also give the parallel vectors for q-32785 and q-127043. In q-32817, the image shows P=(-1,3,2) and Q=(2,4,5), so Q-P=(3,1,3). In q-127065, adding t times the supplied direction to the supplied point gives the parametric equations. In q-127078 and q-70866, setting each symmetric ratio equal to t gives the parametric equations. In q-71028 and q-127405, eliminating t gives the symmetric equations. In q-71035, the zero x direction component requires x=-3 separately, with (y-6)/10=(z+2)/3.
